pages.x: Yugoslavia, the land of the South Slavs, joined together Serbs, Croats, Bosnian Muslims, Slovenes, Macedonians, Montenegrins and Albanians. Its communist leader, Tito, held it together for 35 years. After he died in 1980 the economy faltered, and politicians in each republic began to stir up fear of the others.

Slobodan Milošević rose to power in Serbia by stirring up Serb anger. In 1989, on the 600th anniversary of the battle of Kosovo, he spoke to a vast crowd of Serbs on the old battlefield and warned that armed battles could not be ruled out. Croats, Slovenes and others heard a threat.

In June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Slovenia was free after a war of ten days, but in Croatia, where many Serbs lived, the Yugoslav army and Serb rebels seized nearly a third of the country. The town of Vukovar was shelled to ruins for three months, and when it fell some 200 men were taken from its hospital and shot.

When Bosnia voted for independence in 1992, Bosnian Serb forces under Radovan Karadžić and General Ratko Mladić surrounded its capital, Sarajevo. For almost four years, the longest siege of a capital in modern times, snipers and shells killed people queuing for bread and water. More than 10,000 people died, among them over 1,500 children.

Across Bosnia armed men drove people of other groups out of their homes, burned their villages, and held prisoners in camps where many were tortured and killed. A new phrase, ethnic cleansing, entered the language. Serb forces did most of it, but Croat and Bosnian Muslim forces committed crimes too. About 100,000 people died in Bosnia, and two million fled.

In July 1995 Mladić's troops overran Srebrenica, a town the UN had declared a safe area, guarded by a few hundred lightly armed Dutch peacekeepers. The women and children were bused away. Over a few days the men and boys were murdered and buried in mass graves. International judges ruled it genocide.

After Srebrenica, and a shell that killed dozens in a Sarajevo market, NATO bombed the Bosnian Serbs, while Croatia's army swept back through its lost lands and some 200,000 Serbs fled. In November 1995 the leaders met at an air base in Dayton, Ohio, and agreed to keep Bosnia one country, split into two parts.

In 1998 war came to Kosovo, a province of Serbia where most people were Albanian. As Serb forces drove out hundreds of thousands of Albanians, NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days in 1999, until Milošević pulled his troops out. In 2000 he was overthrown by his own people, and in 2008 Kosovo declared independence.

Seven countries, counting Kosovo, now stand where Yugoslavia was. The wars killed about 130,000 people and brought words like genocide and concentration camp back to Europe. A UN court in The Hague tried their leaders: Milošević died during his trial, and Karadžić and Mladić were jailed for life.
pts: Their leaders were tried in The Hague
